strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine flaw in prior color-equivariant networks (LCER, Yang et al. 2024), namely that modeling bounded saturation/luminance as 1D translations requires clipping/zero-padding, which breaks exact equivariance. The empirical demonstration (lifting error six orders of magnitude lower, Figure 4; equivariance error 4.66e-6 vs 0.445, Figure 3) convincingly substantiates this diagnosis.

The core idea — using a double-cover to impose cyclic (group) structure on interval-valued quantities so that group convolution applies exactly — is an elegant and reasonably original application of topological covering ideas to a practical architecture design problem, with a nice ablation framing of the method's extension to RGB shifts and scale.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: synthetic controlled settings (3D Shapes with hue/saturation/luminance/HSL shifts), small NORB lighting shifts, six natural image datasets with shifted test sets, Camelyon17 medical imaging, multiple seeds (3-5), parameter-matched comparisons against ResNet, CEConv, and LCER, and an analysis of the trade-off between group order and filter capacity (Appendix C.1).

The analysis of lifting coverage (Section 5.4, entropy-based coverage) provides a principled, data-driven way to select group order, connecting the degenerate-lifting phenomenon to empirical accuracy peaks (hue-shift MNIST), which is a thoughtful contribution beyond the main method.
Honest limitations discussion (computational expense of GCNNs) and mostly reproducible detail (hyperparameters, seeds, hardware, dataset splits in Appendix D).
weaknesses: Mathematical rigor of the central construction is lacking. The map π(θ) = (c/2) sin θ is called a 'covering' of the interval, but sin θ has vanishing derivative at its extrema and is not a local homeomorphism, so it is not a covering map in the standard topological sense; the interval is also not homeomorphic to a quotient of T¹ by a group action. The lifting of a saturation value xs ∈ [0,c] to an angle requires a branch choice (inverse sine is two-valued), and this choice — which is the crux of the 'double-cover' — is never made precise. Equivariance of the HSL group convolution is asserted ('It can be shown') rather than proven; only group-axiom verifications for the discretized cyclic sets are provided in the appendix, which are trivial and somewhat padded.

The semantic validity of cyclic saturation/luminance is under-examined. Wrapping luminance makes black and white equivalent under the group action, and the paper's own Figure 1 shows an artifact of this design (a white background lifts to a black/gray background under luminance lifting) — precisely the kind of spurious artifact the method claims to eliminate relative to clipping. A discussion of when cyclic structure is a perceptually justified prior versus merely mathematically convenient is missing.

Several presentation issues undermine confidence: apparent typos in Equation (24) (mixing 'gi' with 'αi' in the scale group action); the misspelling 'hypertorodoidal' in the introduction; incomplete sentence in Appendix D.5 ('Example images are shown in Figure'); and the extension experiments (RGB shift, scale equivariance) are only qualitative commutativity checks without quantitative error or downstream-task evidence.

Duplicated numerical results raise questions: in Tables 5, 6, and 7 the T³CEN-H4 rows are identical to LCER-H4 rows to every digit. This is plausibly intentional (T³CEN's hue lifting follows Yang et al. exactly, so the models coincide) but is never stated, leaving the reader unable to distinguish a copy-paste error from a deliberate equivalence.

The claimed generality ('perfectly equivariant to shifts in hue, saturation, and luminance') is only exact for the discrete group actions defined; continuous/interpolated shifts, anti-aliasing of the group convolution, and discretization effects are not analyzed, and the 4.66e-6 equivariance error is attributed to computation without analysis of where it arises.

Empirical gains over the strongest baseline (LCER) are mixed in places: on vanilla datasets T³CEN-H4 ties LCER-H4 exactly and several higher-order T³CEN variants underperform lower-order ones due to the filter-reduction scheme (acknowledged by the authors), so the practical benefit rests mainly on the saturation/luminance-shifted settings.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: lifting interval-valued quantities (saturation, luminance) to a cyclic space to obtain exact group structure for color GCNNs is a natural and somewhat novel way to remove the clipping artifacts of prior work (Yang et al., 2024).

Broad empirical evaluation across synthetic (3D Shapes, small NORB, hue-shift MNIST) and real datasets (Camelyon17, CIFAR, Caltech-101, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, STL-10), with parameter-matched baselines and multiple random seeds.
The analysis of degenerate lifting and the entropy-based heuristic for selecting group order (Section 5.4) is a thoughtful addition that addresses a real failure mode of the proposed lifting.
The observation that LCER's equivariance error and classification accuracy trade off against each other via zero-padding (Appendix C.2) is an insightful diagnostic of the prior method.
weaknesses: The central mathematical claim is incorrect: the map π(θ) = (c/2) sin θ is called a 'double-cover' and a covering map, but it is not a covering. A covering must be a local homeomorphism; sin θ has critical points at the fold (θ = ±π/2) where the map is not locally invertible. It is a fold map, not a covering. Since 'a truly equivariant architecture' built on 'topological covering' is the paper's headline contribution, this is a fundamental flaw.

The group action on images (Eq. 8, Eq. 28) is not a well-defined group action in the image domain: a saturation value in the interval has two preimages on the circle with different shift behavior, so shifting an already-transformed image does not compose as φ_s(s_j, φ_s(s_i, x)) = φ_s(s_i + s_j, x). Consequently the claimed 'perfect equivariance to shifts in saturation and luminance' of the images is not established; exact equivariance holds only trivially for functions on the abstract group (as in any GCNN), and the induced image transformation is a nonlinear wrap-around, not a perceptual shift.

The claimed extension to scale equivariance (Eq. 24) is incoherent: it contains an undefined variable (g_i vs α_i) and applies the sine covering to pixel coordinates, which has no meaningful interpretation as scaling. This extension is supported only by a qualitative figure, and the RGB extension is acknowledged to be degenerate on all channels. Both 'going beyond color' claims (abstract, conclusion) are thus substantially oversold.

Suspicious duplicated results: T³CEN-H4 and LCER-H4 rows are numerically identical in Table 5 and Table 7 across all six datasets, and near-identical in Table 1. This is either a copy-paste error or an unexplained consequence of the hue lifting being shared with LCER; either way it undermines confidence in the experimental reporting.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: numerous typos ('hypertorodoidal', 'an input images', incomplete sentences such as 'Example images are shown in Figure'), a citation error (3D Shapes attributed to Krause et al., 2013 in Appendix D but Kim & Mnih, 2018 in Section 5.1), inconsistent naming (T³CEN vs T⁴CEN), and an appendix that pads pages with a trivial proof that modular addition is associative/invertible.

Several empirical claims are overstated relative to the evidence: 'significantly better' in Table 2 where differences are 0.04 error; odd results (e.g., ResNet-aug degrading CIFAR-10 luminance-shift error from 36.79 to 63.63) go undiscussed; equivariance error is only quantitatively measured for the saturation channel on synthetic data.

The semantic justification for treating saturation and luminance as cyclic (values near 0 wrapping to values near c, and the N/2+1 useful-representation degeneracy reducing effective capacity) is underexplored relative to how central it is to the method's validity; the limitations section discusses only compute cost.
No code release is mentioned, and reproducibility of the Camelyon17 pipeline (patient-level WSI classification details) is thin.

strengths: The core observation is convincing: modeling interval-valued quantities (saturation, luminance) with a translation group forces clipping/zero-padding artifacts, and the paper convincingly demonstrates that replacing this with a cyclic structure reduces measured saturation equivariance error from 0.445 to 4.66e-6 and lifting error by six orders of magnitude (Figures 3, 4).

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this literature: synthetic 3D Shapes variants (hue, saturation, HSL), small NORB, Camelyon17, and six natural-image benchmarks, with parameter-matched baselines (ResNet, CEConv, LCER), multiple random seeds, and reported standard deviations.

The analysis in Section 5.4 of lifting coverage, degenerate cases, and entropy-based selection of group order is a genuinely useful practical contribution and is supported by the MNIST order-sweep experiment (Appendix C.1).
The limitations section honestly addresses the computational expense of GCNNs rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The central mathematical claim is not correct as stated. The map π(θ) = (c/2) sin θ from T¹ onto the interval is not a covering map: it fails to be a local homeomorphism at the fold points (θ = π/2, 3π/2), and no covering map from a connected T¹ onto a contractible interval exists. Calling this a 'double-cover' and claiming 'perfect equivariance via topological covering' overstates the rigor of the construction; it is a fold map, and the paper's own 'degenerate lifting' analysis (Section 5.4) shows the pathologies that result.

The induced group action on images appears ill-defined. Because the lift from the interval to the circle is two-to-one, a saturation value xs admits two preimage angles, so the action φs(si, x) = (xh, π((xs + si) mod 2π), xl) in Equation (8) depends on an unspecified choice of lift. The paper never states how this ambiguity is resolved, which undermines the theoretical guarantee of exact equivariance that motivates the whole approach.

The motivation contains an inaccurate claim: Section 3 states GCNNs 'require that symmetry transformation is a finite group,' contradicting the continuous-group convolution networks the paper itself cites (Worrall et al., 2017; scale-equivariant networks).

The RGB and scale extensions are thin and partially erroneous. Equation (24) mixes 'gi' where the scale element αi is expected, and both extensions are evaluated only qualitatively via feature-map commutativity pictures (Figure 7), with no quantitative or downstream-task evidence.

Several result tables show T³CEN entries identical to LCER entries to every decimal (T³CEN-H4 vs. LCER-H4 in Tables 5 and 7; T³CEN-H3 vs. LCER-H3 in Table 1), despite being averaged over three seeds. This is either a copy-paste error or the hue-only variant is exactly the LCER architecture; either way it requires clarification and casts doubt on table preparation.

Presentation is sloppy for a main-track submission: 'hypertorodoidal' for 'hypertoroidal', grammatical errors ('can convolved', 'An input images', an incomplete sentence 'shown in Figure'), inconsistent naming (T³CEN vs. T⁴CEN) within Figure 7 and its caption, and mislabeled references (3D Shapes attributed to Krause et al., 2013, which is Stanford Cars).

Statistical support for some headline claims is weak: the best Camelyon17 result (T³CEN-S4, 12.11) has high variance, several T³CEN variants underperform LCER (e.g., luminance-shifted CIFAR rows in Table 5), and no significance testing is provided.
No code release is mentioned, and reproducibility of the equivariance experiments depends on the unspecified lifting choices flagged above.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: replacing the clipped translation-group treatment of interval-valued color channels (saturation, luminance) in LCER (Yang et al., 2024) with a double-cover lift to the circle, which yields genuinely (not approximately) equivariant group actions. The empirical demonstration of this is convincing: saturation equivariance error drops from 0.445 (LCER) to ~4.66e-6 (Figure 3, Figure 10), and lifting error is six orders of magnitude lower (Figure 4).

The evaluation is broad and mostly well-designed: synthetic 3D Shapes with hue/saturation/HSL shifts, small NORB for luminance, six real image datasets with shifted test sets, and Camelyon17 for a real-world color-imbalance setting. Improvements over ResNet, augmentation baselines, CEConv, and LCER are consistent where the claimed symmetry is relevant.

The paper is unusually honest about failure modes. Section 5.5 explicitly characterizes and quantifies when color equivariance hurts (color as the signal on KUTomaData; no distribution shift on hue-shifted MNIST), and Appendix C.1/C.2 analyzes the capacity/order trade-off and the tension between equivariance error and accuracy for the baseline. This kind of boundary-mapping strengthens the contribution's usefulness.

Reproducibility is treated seriously: multiple random seeds per experiment, full hyperparameter tables, dataset construction details, and a compute/memory benchmark (Table 12) showing GCNN cost is comparable to an equivalent widened filter bank.
The demonstrated generality of the lifting (RGB channels, spatial scale) suggests the construction is a reusable tool beyond color, even though those extensions are only sketched qualitatively.
weaknesses: Mathematical rigor is looser than the claims suggest. The map π(θ) = (c/2)sin θ is called a 'double-cover' of the interval, but it is not a covering map in the strict topological sense (it is 2-to-1 generically and degenerates at the extrema), and 'the inverse of π' is multi-valued; the paper relies on intuition rather than a precise statement. The claimed group actions on images (e.g., Eq. 8) also mix units — xs is an interval value while si is an angle — so it is unclear how the lifted angle is obtained without a formally defined branch of the inverse.

The redundancy problem is significant and only partially addressed: at certain input values the lift produces duplicated representations, and the paper's own entropy analysis shows coverage is input-dependent. This means 'perfect equivariance' is bought at the cost of information loss for some inputs, a trade-off that deserves deeper analysis than the ~1% redundancy statistics in Table 10.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: two consecutive sections are both titled 'Background' (Sections 3 and 4); the scale-equivariance action in Eq. (24) contains an apparent typo (gi instead of αi); the RGB/scale extensions are validated only qualitatively via feature-map commutativity plots rather than quantitative equivariance error; and there are repeated typos and grammar issues throughout ('hypertorodoidal', 'focuses on', 'can convolved').

Novelty is moderate. The construction is a reparameterization trick (lift interval to circle via a sinusoid) applied within an existing GCNN framework, with the hue machinery taken directly from Yang et al. (2024). The main intellectual contribution is recognizing and fixing the clipping artifact, which is real but incremental.

Some experimental results are not as clean as the headline claims: on the luminance-shifted real datasets (Table 6, bottom), T³CEN variants do not consistently dominate (e.g., Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets), and the best Camelyon17 configuration (S4) is not the full HSL model, weakening the 'full hypertoroidal' story. Perfect 0.00 (0.00) errors in several tables also suggest the synthetic shift protocols exactly match the discretized group, which inflates the practical significance.

No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of an architecture whose implementation details (e.g., handling of the multi-valued inverse in the lift) are not fully specified in the text.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: lifting interval-valued quantities (saturation, luminance) to the circle via a double-cover so that group convolution applies, resolving the value-clipping artifacts of Yang et al. (2024). This is a genuine, if incremental, conceptual improvement over prior color-equivariant architectures.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this line of work: synthetic equivariance-error measurements (Fig. 3, 4), multiple OOD color-shift benchmarks (3D Shapes variants, small NORB, Camelyon17), and six natural-image datasets with augmentation baselines (Tables 5-6), with multiple random seeds and parameter-matched comparisons.

The limitations section (Sec. 5.5) is honest and unusually good: it explicitly characterizes when color equivariance helps and when it hurts (color-as-signal, no distribution shift) and quantifies both failure modes, which is more self-critical than most equivariance papers.

The entropy-based analysis of lifting coverage (Sec. 5.4, Figs. 5-6) is a nice practical contribution, giving a principled way to select group order, and is validated against the empirical accuracy-order curve in Appendix C.1.
Computational costs (memory, it/s in Table 12) and implementation details (seeds, hardware, hyperparameters) are reported, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central mathematical claim is stated loosely and not fully supported. The paper calls π(θ) = (c/2)sin θ a 'double-cover' of the interval and claims the resulting space is 'isomorphic to T¹', but a covering map requires even coverage; a map from T¹ to an interval with boundary cannot be a covering map in the topological sense (endpoints are not evenly covered, and the preimage structure degenerates). Worse, the inverse is not single-valued: two angles map to the same interval value, so the 'lifting' in Eq. (8) is not invertible, and the group action on interval-valued image channels mixes angle and interval coordinates (xs is an interval value but is treated as an angle in Eq. (8)). The paper's 'perfect' equivariance is therefore equivariance to a cyclic wrap-around action on the lifted representation, which is a different (and arguably weaker) statement than equivariance to physical saturation/luminance shifts. The claimed proof burden is never met: Sec. 4 states 'It can be shown that the HSL group convolution is equivariant' with no proof anywhere, while the appendix spends pages proving trivial facts (associativity of modular addition) that need no proof.

The construction wastes half the representation: the authors themselves show (Eq. 19, Sec. 5.4) that lifted representations are redundant for at least half the orbit, and that natural datasets incur ~0.6-0.9% fully/partially redundant pixels (Table 10). The paper does not adequately discuss how the duplicated orbit elements affect learning or whether the redundancy explains the non-monotonic accuracy-vs-order behavior.

Presentation quality is poor for a main-track submission: two sections are both titled 'Background' (Secs. 3 and 4); there are repeated typos ('hypertorodoidal', 'T⁴CEN' vs T³CEN, 'architectures have focuses'); Figure 5's caption/labeling is confused (two different 'Figure 5' panels across pages 7); Figure 8's caption references T³CEN and T⁴CEN inconsistently; Eq. (24) mixes gi and αi; Appendix D.5 has a truncated sentence ('Example images are shown in Figure'); the Caltech-101 citation is malformed. These errors suggest insufficient care and undermine confidence in the technical details.

A related-work claim is factually wrong: Sec. 3 states GCNNs 'require that symmetry transformation is a finite group,' yet the same paragraph and the cited literature (Worrall et al. 2017; Esteves et al. 2018; Cohen et al. 2019a) treat continuous groups. This misstatement is used to motivate the paper, which is concerning.

Some experimental claims are oversold relative to the tables. Table 2 shows LCER-S3 at 0.00/0.00/0.04 vs T³CEN-S3 at 0.00/0.00/0.00 — hardly 'significantly better classification accuracy than all baselines.' T³CEN-H4 rows in Tables 6 and 9 are numerically identical to LCER-H4 rows, which the text does not explain (presumably identical architecture, but as reported it looks like copy-paste). Table 3's OOD gains (e.g., 31.53 error on A/C for the best model) are large in relative terms but still far from strong performance.

The claimed generalization beyond color is thin: the RGB and scale applications (Sec. 6, Eqs. 20-24) are qualitative sketches only — no quantitative results, no baselines, and Eq. (24) contains errors — so the abstract's claim that the lifting 'can also extend to geometric transformations such as scale' is not substantiated.

Novelty is modest relative to Yang et al. (2024): the hue machinery is adopted directly, and the contribution reduces to replacing the translation-group lifting of saturation/luminance with a cyclic one. The paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is fundamentally new versus an engineering fix.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: prior color-equivariant networks (LCER, Yang et al. 2024) model interval-valued saturation/luminance with a translation group, requiring clipping and zero-padding that break exact equivariance; this paper instead lifts interval-valued quantities to the circle, giving a cyclic group on which group convolution is exactly equivariant.

The empirical evidence for the central claim is strong: the saturation equivariance error drops from 0.445 (LCER) to 4.66e-6, and the lifting-error experiment (Figure 4, six orders of magnitude reduction) directly isolates the source of LCER's artifacts.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive: controlled synthetic tests (3D Shapes with hue/saturation/HSL shifts), small NORB for luminance, Camelyon17 as a real medical imaging task with color imbalance, and six natural image datasets with shifted test sets against augmentation baselines (AugMix, DeepAugment, Planckian Jitter). Multiple random seeds are reported, parameter counts are matched, and computational cost/memory is honestly reported (Table 12).

The paper is refreshingly honest about when its approach fails: Section 5.5 explicitly characterizes and quantifies the two failure modes (color-as-signal on KUTomaData; capacity cost when there is no distribution shift on MNIST). This kind of boundary analysis strengthens trust in the contribution.

The coverage/entropy analysis (Figures 5-6, Appendix C.1) connecting group order selection to dataset statistics is a nice practical contribution, and the qualitative extensions to RGB and scale suggest the lifting layer is a reusable tool rather than a color-specific trick.
weaknesses: The central mathematical framing is imprecise. The map pi(theta) = (c/2) sin(theta) from T^1 to the interval is called a 'double-cover', but it is not a covering map in the topological sense: it has critical points (derivative zero) at the extreme values, so it fails the local-homeomorphism/evenness condition the paper itself cites. In fact, since the interval is simply connected, no nontrivial connected covering of it exists. The construction is really a folded/wrapping parametrization; the theory should be restated accordingly, and the 'perfect equivariance via covering' claim reframed (the practical equivariance comes from the cyclic group structure on the discretized circle, which does hold).

The group action on images (Eq. 8) is not well defined as written: xs is an interval value but si is an angle, so 'xs + si (mod 2pi)' mixes domains. Applying the action requires first lifting xs to an angle via the (two-valued) inverse of pi, and the paper never specifies which branch is chosen or how this affects the composition axioms near the fold points. This is glossed over and is exactly where the 'redundant representations' arise; a rigorous treatment of the lifting choice is missing.

Several technical inconsistencies and typos undermine confidence: Eq. 3 uses hue mod 255 while Appendix B uses 2pi k/N; Eq. 24 defines the scale action with 'px + gi' instead of the scale parameter alpha_i, and the 'scale equivariance' demo acts by shifting pixel coordinates rather than scaling; Sections 3 and 4 are both titled 'Background'; Figure 7/8 text alternates between T^3CEN and T^4CEN; 'hypertorodoidal' and other typos appear throughout.

The theoretical claim of exact equivariance of the HSL group convolution (Eq. 16, 'it can be shown') is asserted without a proof in the main text or appendix; given that the proof is the paper's central claim, an explicit statement/proof of the equivariance theorem for the product group should be included.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a paper whose value lies in an implementable layer; implementation details are otherwise good (hyperparameters, seeds, hardware).

On the strongest real-world result (Camelyon17), the best configuration is saturation-only (S4, 12.11); the full H4S4L4 model (19.97) underperforms it, and the explanation (filter-depth reduction) is plausible but only indirectly analyzed, so the benefit of the full hypertoroidal structure on real data is less clear than the synthetic results suggest.
